    #89720. Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4365 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try fresh things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try fresh things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    It has been revealed that most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, declared it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    In a recent development, I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    For many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” stated Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money promptly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” mentioned María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    Recent findings suggest that “They said to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    Industry observers note that first-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, remarked Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    In a recent development, “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” mentioned Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    According to recent reports, the Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” remarked Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    The funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin noted. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” mentioned Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” noted Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased new software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very quickly,” he noted, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    According to recent reports, the Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a latest website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    The Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a upcoming media kit, which Olson stated has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    The open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr mentioned. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to proposal ahead.

    Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    The Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” said Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the latest hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    According to recent reports, the Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    The funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz noted.

    The Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve organization housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, said editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    It has been revealed that the turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    It has been revealed that sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” said Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    It has been revealed that the World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr said. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    According to recent reports, other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    EcoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    The salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz noted. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she remarked, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    In a recent development, beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she said. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she said, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    Sources indicate that planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she mentioned.

    Ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she mentioned. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    NotiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    It has been revealed that california’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    In Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    According to recent reports, for instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer noted, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    Sources indicate that planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak noted. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak said. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    Sources indicate that anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he mentioned, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Sources indicate that press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting tech giant Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

    It has been revealed that the coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants stated the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving rapidly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    This was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” stated Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear plan. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    It has been revealed that A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he stated it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    According to recent reports, sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    Industry observers note that in addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin remarked 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    Sources indicate that stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar mentioned, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    Sources indicate that to small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    So several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she mentioned.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    Recent findings suggest that since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition notes it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    When Press Forward first unveiled the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee noted it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin remarked. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    The argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher said. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    Sources indicate that young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    According to recent reports, “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he said. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    It has been revealed that young mentioned he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    Industry observers note that right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak remarked the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health problems in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    As for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    Sources indicate that LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he noted, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person said, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer said.

    Sources indicate that “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Sandpoint Reader, Olson remarked, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    Sources indicate that “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she said. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • YouTube has come under fire in the past for how it handles content posted by people suspected of heinous crimes, but its policy has remained the same: It will only terminate a channel if someone is convicted in a court of law, and if their YouTube content is directly related to their crime.
    • Now, the platform has refused a request from the Prison Service of England and Wales to remove content from Russell Brand‘s channel.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    YouTube has come under fire in the past for how it handles content posted by people suspected of heinous crimes, but its policy has remained the same: It will only terminate a channel if someone is convicted in a court of law, and if their YouTube content is directly related to their crime.

    Now, the platform has refused a request from the Prison Service of England and Wales to remove content from Russell Brand‘s channel.

    The comedian and actor will be in prison for over a decade after being convicted of three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape, stemming attacks on four different women. Presiding British High Court judge Mr Justice Bennathan described Brand as a “sexual predator” whose behavior demonstrated a “series of lies” and “staggering arrogance.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In the upload, Brand asserts innocence, telling viewers, “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.”.

    Authorities contacted YouTube via “an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material,” per the BBC, to ask that Brand’s video be removed.

    But YouTube isn’t willing to scrub it–at least not yet.

    “We are aware of the new content and our teams are investigating,” a spokesperson from YouTube parent Google told the BBC. “We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetize on YouTube since then.”.

    That’s a pretty typical order of operations for YouTube. In past cases with creators like Adnan Ahmed, Austin Jones, and Ian Rylett, YouTube suspended monetization on their channels when allegations surfaced and the legal process began, and then terminated their channels once convictions were filed.

    He also holds Christianity-themed “Sunday services” with Gallacher.

    It has been revealed that the assaults Brand was convicted for all happened before 2009; he made his YouTube channel in 2007, but didn’t start uploading videos until 2012. YouTube could potentially claim they’re not related based on timeline alone, since Brand–who was already a celebrity outside of YouTube–didn’t use his channel or digital clout to connect with his victims.

    So the question here is: Does YouTube amend its policies to ban convicted criminals–or specifically convicted sex offenders–from posting on its platform? What if their fresh content is directly related to their crimes, as Brand’s is?

    United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham got involved after YouTube’s initial denial, telling the platform (and other socmed platforms) to “show some decency and take these videos down.”.

    “[It’s] time that we focus on the victims and think about them,” he added, instead of “hearing from a convicted criminal.”.

    “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down,” Burnham added. “Why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”.

    The attention on YouTube’s refusal has sparked a bit of a Streisand effect. Commenters are flocking to Brand’s video, sneering at Burnham, the U.K. government, and activists for their attempts to remove it.

    “Had no intention to watch until the government told me not to,” one top-liked comment indicates.

    “If the government tells you not to watch a video, you really need to watch that video to find out why,” another indicates.

    Sources indicate that other socmed platforms have cut Brand off. Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp–all owned by Meta–have culled his accounts, thanks to policies that prohobit convicted sex offenders from owning and/or operating accounts.

    Our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end people, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk. We are hiring a Security Engineer to build and run our vulnerability management and security operations program. Vulnerability management is a core capability for keeping our security posture strong as the platform and the tech giant grow: knowing what we run, finding what is exposed, and getting the right fixes shipped quickly. It also underpins our customer commitments and the compliance programs we are building. Our program is early, and you will shape it. You will join a small Trust team that covers security, IT and compliance, and you will own this program end to end from your first week.

    think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.

    take an automation-first and pragmatic approach to risk mitigation.

    translate security concerns into engineering action.

    can clearly explain complex technical concepts to others.

    are a fast learner and thrive in ambiguity.

    Select, deploy and operationalize scanning tooling across our production assets.

    Run vulnerability management end to end: triage, severity in our environment, owner assignment, remediation SLAs and reporting.

    Build engineering-first triage and remediation workflows that fit how our engineering teams already work, and automate the routing and follow-up.

    Build a remediation dashboard that engineering and leadership read and act on.

    Automate collection of the vulnerability management evidence our compliance programs depend on, in partnership with our Compliance team.

    Build automation, including agentic tooling, that removes manual security operations work and keeps pace with engineering growth.

    5+ years in security engineering, security operations or software engineering, with a significant share of that focused on security.

    Hands-on experience building or running a vulnerability management program or software security tooling (SCA, container, cloud or host scanning).

    An engineering-first approach to triage and remediation: you get findings fixed by making the fix easy to ship.

    The judgment to set a finding's real severity in our environment, using CVSS as one input.

    Strong scripting and automation skills in a language such as Go or Python, and comfort reading infrastructure as code such as Terraform.

    A pragmatic approach to risk: you can explain why a finding matters to the business and how fast it needs to be fixed.

    Experience with real-time media, networking or WebRTC systems.

    Experience supporting compliance audits such as HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001 or SOC 2.

    Incident response or application security experience.

    Experience in AI security, such as securing LLM applications or agent infrastructure.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    #89709. YouTube bows out of World Cup rights race; Netflix might step up

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    YouTube bows out of World Cup rights race; Netflix might step up

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (384 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that youTube was an official “Preferred Platform” for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, and it worked to make the partnership a high scorer.
    • It also exercised the broadcast rights that came along with being a Preferred Platform: By the time Spain took it all home, YouTube’s World Cup content had drawn nearly 2 billion unique viewers, 550 million of whom tuned in from their TV sets and bumped YouTube’s Nielsen numbers.
    • But that success apparently isn’t enough of a carrot for YouTube to go bigger and bid for TV rights to future World Cups.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that youTube was an official “Preferred Platform” for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, and it worked to make the partnership a high scorer. It tapped creators to film promo content, then brought them pitchside to film dozens of videos at the tournament’s top matches around the world.

    It also exercised the broadcast rights that came along with being a Preferred Platform: By the time Spain took it all home, YouTube’s World Cup content had drawn nearly 2 billion unique viewers, 550 million of whom tuned in from their TV sets and bumped YouTube’s Nielsen numbers.

    But that success apparently isn’t enough of a carrot for YouTube to go bigger and bid for TV rights to future World Cups.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to Atlantic sports columnist Andrew Marchand, YouTube declined to submit a bid for American broadcast rights to the 2030 and 2034 World Cups.

    There were rumors that YouTube planned to go out for rights, but a source familiar with the matter confirmed to Marchand that YouTube is not tossing its hat in the ring.

    It has been revealed that it’s not alone: Apple, ESPN, NBC, and the newly formed Skydance have also declined to bid. Between their various subsidiaries, that knocks out chances of the World Cups airing on CBS, TNT Sports, Paramount+, HBO Max, and Telemundo.

    According to recent reports, so who does want the rights? Marchand reports Fox–which had the rights for 2026–is going out for them. But, perhaps surprisingly, the other top frontrunner seems to be Netflix.

    Or maybe it’s not so surprising–Netflix already has rights to the 2027 Women’s World Cup, and we know it’s willing to pay massive for exclusive sporting events, so maybe the men’s Cup is exactly the complement it’s looking for.

    We don’t know what the winner will end up paying here, but Fox paid $485 million to air the 2026 tourney in the U.S. Netflix did say it expects to close out the year spending money on developing original content and investing in sports (and now it has freer cash considering its failed bid to buy Warner Bros. Discovery). The World Cup just might be one of those investments.

    Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

    In a recent development, when I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia remarked “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

    I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

    Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

    That article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which debuted a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

    Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It reveals that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

    Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

    It has been revealed that musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a newly introduced version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had substantial aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia indicates edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors demonstrated Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s vital and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches.

    Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”).

    Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia.

    Sources indicate that grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version.

    Sources indicate that grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty.

    Recent findings suggest that musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR.

    Sources indicate that my big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok highlights that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles.

    After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities.

    Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

    According to recent reports, right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each organization’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft noted they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

    Recent findings suggest that anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI notes it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

    Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the organization supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    Sources indicate that topper Guild is getting into the animation game. Content creator Topper Guild is teaming up with animation company Toonstar to create an original series, which is set to premiere on YouTube. “Animation is a medium I’ve always wanted to work in, but I didn’t think it was possible to maintain that same pace my fans expect, or retain the creative control I have with my live-action content,” Guild said. “But Toonstar changed that. They’re unlocking animation for the creator economy.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Industry observers note that kane Parsons is going from Backrooms to BAFTA. YouTuber-turned-filmmaker Kane Parsons has been named as one of 14 creatives participating in BAFTA North America’s 2026 Breakthrough US cohort. The Backrooms director will join the program alongside rising entertainment icons like Heated Rivalry’s Connor Storrie and The ‘Burbs creator Celeste Hughey.

    Entrepreneurs On Fire has been acquired. John Lee Dumas has reportedly agreed to sell the firm behind his business podcast, Entrepreneurs On Fire, to PR firm Pathos Communications for $3 million in cash, plus up to $6 million in “performance payments.” Dumas will continue to host the show as part of a three-year deal.

    According to recent reports, youTube could pay billions over child safety concerns. Sources familiar with the matter reportedly told Bloomberg that YouTube is preparing to settle a wave of lawsuits regarding its allegedly “addictive” design by paying roughly $3 billion to thousands of school districts.

    TikTok dropped some significant stats in its 2026 Music Impact Report. According to a study commissioned by TikTok from Luminate, 94% of songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 last year went viral on TikTok first—a ten-percentage-point jump from 2024. The report also noted that songs “that go viral on TikTok spend four times longer on the Billboard Global 200 than those without a viral moment.”.

    A Meta vet is coming to OnlyFans. Whitney Rosenthal is coming aboard as OnlyFans’ first global head of creator partnerships. The exec previously worked at Meta and YouTube; most recently, she served as vice president of global creator podcast platforms at Podimo.

    Streaming platforms are going all in on creator content. New data from Ampere Analysis highlights that U.S. streaming services debuted over 3,700 hours of “creator-led programming” in Q3 2026, up from 1,934 in the previous quarter. Distribution of new creator-led content on SVOD services also rose 75% over the last quarter, with Amazon Prime Video alone contributing over 230 hours (per Net Influencer).

    GTA VI made billions on day one. Rockstar Games declared Friday that Grand Theft Auto VI hit $3.79 billion during its first day of retail sales, “setting a upcoming record for entertainment across any medium, and becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.”.

    Industry observers note that A microdrama studio will produce content for Black audiences. NBCUniversal and HarbourView Equity Partners are throwing their financial weight behind June, a microdrama studio introduced by Will and Dom Packer. The studio will focus on the development, production, and acquisition of original vertical dramas aimed at Black viewers.

    Freeman & Forrest has a newly introduced majority owner. Falfurrias Management Partners has made a majority investment in B2B influencer marketing firm Freeman & Forrest. Co-founder Emily Freeman will stay on board as CEO, while co-founder Forrest Brazeal will continue in his role as president.

    Sources indicate that e.l.f. set a world record at TwitchCon. e.l.f. Cosmetics made history at TwitchCon 2026 by breaking the Guinness World Record for most people applying make-up simultaneously. The beauty brand’s massive GRWM included 733 in-person participants—and that was only the start of e.l.f.’s onsite activations at the con.

    Lifetime is turning a viral friendship into a film. In 2016, Wanda Dench and Jamal Hinton spread holiday cheer across the internet by sharing the heartwarming story of how an accidental text turned into an invitation to Thanksgiving dinner. Ten years later, Dench and Hinton have turned their shared Thanksgivings into an annual tradition—and now, Lifetime is turning it into a movie.

    In a recent development, the Denver Broncos are tapping into the power of anime. The anime horse girls of Umamusume: Pretty Derby have become a familiar sight for sports fans in recent months, with appearances at events ranging from Grand Prix de Paris to Japan’s Super GT championship. Now—as part of an official collaboration with the Denver Broncos—two of the anime’s most recognizable characters will be on hand to support the team at Empower Field when they face the Miami Dolphins next month.

    #1 I finally saw quantum physics with my own eyes… Channel: Veritasium Brand: Ground News Views: 19,817,457.

    Industry observers note that it’s not every day you get to see someone push the boundaries of physics. Veritasium secures a regular spot in our top 5 with his science deep dives, and this one might be among his best yet.

    Even for working scientists, accessing equipment for quantum physics experiments can be a tough time–so the Veritasium team’s partnership with the Gravity Laboratory at the University of Nottingham allowed them to give the world a vicarious look at what happens to helium when you just don’t stop cooling it down.

    The Gravity Lab’s gear allowed Veritasium–and now, any YouTube viewer–to observe helium’s transformation into a superfluid in real time, and discuss how superfluidity can be applied in fields like astrophysics.

    These kinds of videos remind me the universe is pretty cool, and even when things aren’t so hot on Earth (metaphorically speaking), there are countless galaxies dancing around us, full of potential.

    Recent findings suggest that oh, also, this video is sponsored by Ground News, which compares various news sources and evaluates them for potential biases. Its sponsorships spiked in the leadup to the midterm elections, but even after Voting Day, we’re still seeing decent numbers: It paid for ~20 other videos this week.

    We go from Veritasium letting viewers do physics vicariously to Jessica Braun letting viewers shop vicariously. With Black Friday coming up, basically every store is trying to whet shoppers’ appetites, but the economy is tough right now, and not everyone can cut loose with a day of dropping dolla dolla bills.

    It has been revealed that that’s not to say Braun’s vlog is an ultra-luxury haul. It’s an everyday trip around to Target, Walmart, and out for groceries. Her sponsoring brand is equally everyday: smart lighting manufacturer Govee. Someone told me once that color-changing lightbulbs let you instantly paint a room any color you want, for free, and you know what? I’ve found that to be true–and cheap.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    Industry observers note that but not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    It has been revealed that “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    It has been revealed that to reach fresh audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres remarked she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Sources indicate that from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is presently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    In a recent development, another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Industry observers note that mongabay now looks its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    Sources indicate that not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    Recent findings suggest that “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres stated. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he noted. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Industry observers note that today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    It has been revealed that “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.).

    According to recent reports, “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler remarked. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    Sources indicate that part of the problem, he stated, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

You’ll partner closely with Product, Engineering, Sales, Marketing, and Finance to take integrations from idea to launch—and grow their impact long after launch.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins unveiled the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    It has been revealed that but we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one firm or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    According to recent reports, indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    Industry observers note that collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the Fresh Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The Fresh Orleans Bowl.

    I love Latest Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the Upcoming Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in Latest Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and stated it straight up: "No.".

    Recent findings suggest that we asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the Newly introduced Orleans Bowl might be out, several presently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

    Sources indicate that the data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a massive part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Newly introduced York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar stated. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    Industry observers note that redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I stated there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like.     It has been revealed that redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the significant stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

    Sources indicate that my week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

    Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

    In a recent development, I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

    Sources indicate that tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

    Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

    Recent findings suggest that redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    Recent findings suggest that for one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

    A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have said this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

    In a recent development, redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

    Recent findings suggest that redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

    According to recent reports, I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing.
