    #89665. How To Find The Questions Your Customers Ask AI (And Your Keyword Tools Miss)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1828 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    How To Find The Questions Your Customers Ask AI (And Your Keyword Tools Miss)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that in my last article, I made the case that search volume is screening out your best content opportunities.
    • So, this is the practical follow-up.
    • I always start here, because it’s the source most teams overlook, and it’s usually the best one.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that in my last article, I made the case that search volume is screening out your best content opportunities. The short version is that the highest-intent questions your buyers ask are increasingly being said to an AI assistant, and they rarely show up in a keyword tool. Near the end of that piece, I listed a few places to find those questions instead: People Also Ask, forums, your own sales calls and support tickets, and the assistants themselves. That list was only four bullet points, and the most common reply I’ve had since is some version of “OK, but how do I actually do that?”.

    So, this is the practical follow-up. I’ll go through how I collect these questions, how I use Search Console to check which ones are already reaching a site, and how I turn the whole lot into something a content team can work from.

    I always start here, because it’s the source most teams overlook, and it’s usually the best one. Sales calls, discovery calls, support tickets, live chat logs, and the messages people send before booking a demo are all people describing their problem in their own words. That’s very close to how they’d describe it to ChatGPT or Gemini.

    Industry observers note that here’s a real example from a recent discovery call of mine (anonymized, with the details changed enough that you couldn’t identify the business). The prospect was a furniture retailer, and this was roughly how they opened the call:.

    According to recent reports, “We moved to Shopify a couple of years ago and lost a massive chunk of our rankings. Some of it came back, and then we dropped again this year. Is that still the migration, or are our own collection pages competing with each other?”.

    A few minutes later, they asked a second question:.

    Recent findings suggest that “We sell exactly the same products in France and Germany, but those sites barely get any traffic. Do we need completely separate content for each country?”.

    Neither of those would ever appear in a keyword export. The closest you’d get is something like “shopify migration SEO” or “international SEO,” which tells you almost nothing about the actual situation. But if you look at those two questions as a content brief, they’re incredibly specific: a platform, a timeline, two possible causes, and a decision to make.

    This is exactly the kind of question a buyer takes to an assistant, and it’s the kind of question your content should be able to answer.

    If you record your calls (I use Fireflies, but most call recorders produce a transcript you can export), I’d take the last three months of sales and discovery calls and run them through an AI assistant with a prompt like this:.

    “From these call transcripts, list every question the prospect asked or implied. Rewrite each one the way they would phrase it to an AI assistant, and keep their constraints, such as firm size, budget, timeline, platform, and what they’ve already tried. Group similar questions together and note how many calls each group came up in.”.

    The final instruction here is critical. If the same scenario comes up in five separate calls, that’s the closest thing to demand data you’ll get for a question with no search volume, and it’s a lot more persuasive in a meeting than “I think people are asking this.”.

    Sources indicate that you want to be careful with a couple of things here. Strip out names, organization details, and anything identifying before transcripts go into a third-party tool, and make sure your call recording consent covers this kind of use. Also, sales calls skew toward people who are already close to buying, so I’d add support tickets and pre-sale inquiries into the mix to capture earlier-stage questions too.

    Recent findings suggest that your own calls only tell you about people who already found you. Forums help with everyone else.

    According to recent reports, reddit is the obvious one, but Quora, industry Slack and Discord communities, Facebook groups, and review sites such as G2 or Trustpilot can all be just as useful depending on your market. The value usually lies in the opening post, where someone explains their constraints in full, and in the replies, where other people ask the follow-up questions an assistant would also need answered before it could give a decent response.

    Sticking with the migration example, a search like site:reddit.com shopify migration rankings dropped should bring up plenty of threads where store owners describe the same problem in their own words, often with details my prospect didn’t mention, such as redirect complications or how long they waited before panicking.

    Sources indicate that I copy the most relevant threads into a document and run the same extraction prompt over them. That way, forum questions and sales questions end up in the same format, and you can group them together later.

    See also: The Review Gap: Finding Client Opportunities In Competitor Feedback.

    Once you have a set of real questions, the next step is working out what an AI assistant would actually search for when answering them.

    Google is open about the fact that AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a query fan-out technique, issuing multiple related searches to build a single response. You can’t see those searches for a real AI Mode session, but you can get a reasonable approximation through the Gemini API.

    When you use Grounding with Google Search, the API response includes a field called webSearchQueries, which lists the searches the model ran to answer your prompt. Google’s own documentation describes it as useful for understanding the model’s reasoning process.

    Recent findings suggest that if you feed in the first migration question from earlier, you’d expect to see sub-queries covering things like how long rankings take to recover after a Shopify migration, how to check redirects after a re-platform, and how to spot keyword cannibalization between collection pages. Your own output will vary from run to run, but each sub-query is effectively a section your page would need to cover to be useful as a source.

    Recent findings suggest that you don’t need to be technical for this. Go Fish Digital published a walkthrough that runs it through Screaming Frog with a copy-and-paste custom JavaScript snippet and an API key from Google AI Studio. Their version sends each page’s H1, but swapping in your own list of questions is straightforward.

    I want to be clear about what this output is, though. It indicates you how a Gemini model expands a question, which is a fair proxy for Google’s AI features, but it isn’t a record of what AI Mode ran for an actual user. I treat it as a coverage checklist, and I wouldn’t present it to a client as anything more definitive than that.

    In a recent development, for ChatGPT, Perplexity, and the other assistants, the manual route still works fine. Ask each one your question, note which sub-topics it decides to cover and which sources it cites, and compare that against the page that’s supposed to answer it.

    See also: The 2003 Framework That Was Already Doing Query Fan-Out.

    Search Console is better as a validation step than a discovery tool for this, because it highlights you which of these questions are already finding their way to your site.

    Long conversational queries do turn up in the Performance report. Suganthan Mohanadasan has already covered four ways to surface them in a lot of detail, so I’d recommend checking that out if you haven’t already. For a quick look, I use the Custom (regex) option in the Query filter. This pattern returns queries of eight words or more:.

    And this one returns queries that start with a question word:.

    In a recent development, then I compare what comes back against the questions from calls and forums. If the migration scenario demonstrates up as a long query, that’s good confirmation that real people are bringing it to Google. If it doesn’t show up, it could be a coverage gap, or the queries may simply be too rare for Google to show you.

    Industry observers note that that last point is significant because Google anonymizes rare queries, and conversational queries are rare almost by definition. Suganthan found that 57.7% of his impressions sat in the anonymized pool over a 59-day period, so anything you find here is an undercount.

    According to recent reports, if you have access to the generative AI performance report, the pages view is worth a look too. It highlights which of your URLs are already appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode. There’s no query data in it (yet), and sites with few AI impressions may not see the report at all, but it does tell you which pages Google is already comfortable using as a source.

    By now, you’ll have a messy list of questions from several sources. To get it into a shape a content team can actually use, I put everything into one sheet. Here’s how a single row might look, using the migration example:.

    For the priority column, I use the same proxies from my previous column: business value, evidence that the question is being asked, how big the coverage gap is, and whether you can answer it with real specifics. The frequency column feeds straight into the second one.

    Once the sheet is filled in, you’ll usually notice that most of the questions cluster around a handful of situations. Those clusters are your content plan. In my experience, most of them can be handled by strengthening a page you already have, which is quicker than publishing something newly introduced and tends to perform better too.

    I’m aware this is a lot less tidy than sorting a spreadsheet by volume, so I think it’s worth being up front about the limitations.

    Sources indicate that you still won’t have a volume figure next to any of these questions, which means you’re prioritizing on judgment and frequency. Your own calls are biased toward people who already know you exist, so questions from audiences you don’t reach yet will be underrepresented. The Gemini fan-out is an approximation of Google’s behavior, and Search Console only highlights you part of the picture because of anonymization.

    Recent findings suggest that however, I don’t think any of that is a reason not to do it. It just means you should present the output as a well-evidenced shortlist, particularly to stakeholders who are used to seeing a number next to every target or goal.

    If you want somewhere to start right now:.

    Sources indicate that keyword tools are still useful for understanding what people type into a search box. But a growing share of the questions that decide whether a buyer picks you are being asked in a conversation with an assistant, and the good news is that plenty of them are already sitting in your inbox and call recordings.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    Sources indicate that A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    As pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and newly introduced hybrid work schedules.

    #89660. Breaking: How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2852 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture.
    • There’s nothing inherently wrong with it.
    • Sources indicate that I don’t have the energy or the wherewithal to play catch-up every year or two.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI is strangely simple. And we’re overcomplicating it.

    In focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture. As an industry, we’ve got away with poor content for years. Updating the same “best spoons” article three times a week because some other idiot is doing exactly the same thing.

    There’s nothing inherently wrong with it. It’s just too SEO-y. We’re missing a much bigger opportunity by framing it through a really narrow lens.

    Sources indicate that I don’t have the energy or the wherewithal to play catch-up every year or two. So I think of AI search as the ultimate synthesis of your marketing efforts.

    Your positioning, reputation, expertise, content, and presence across the internet are all potential inputs into how AI systems understand and represent you.

    It’s not just about your website anymore.

    I’ve spent a lot of time recently working on AI search, information retrieval, audience research, and discoverability strategies. The more I do, the more convinced I become that we need to approach this as marketers, not SEOs.

    It has been revealed that but don’t build your entire “marketing” strategy around it. I use marketing in the loosest possible sense of the word.

    If you’re in dire need of a refresher, here’s a few parts on the fundamentals of modern information retrieval:.

    There’s one other concept I haven’t written about in detail: query fan-out. Not because it’s not notable, more just because a) it’s pretty dull and b) it isn’t a new concept for SEOs. We’ve been using tools like AlsoAsked for years to understand related questions, adjacent information needs and the wider context surrounding a search.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    But we also need to distinguish between three things:.

    They’re related, but they aren’t interchangeable. Being crawled doesn’t guarantee inclusion in training data. Being retrieved doesn’t guarantee a citation. And a citation doesn’t guarantee commercial value.

    It has been revealed that understanding these mechanisms is important – mainly just so you can answer the brain-dead questions people ask you about AI. Building your entire marketing strategy around their current implementation is the action of a halfwit.

    It has been revealed that models, retrieval systems, and interfaces will change. An owned audience is a considerably more durable investment. So build one.

    It has been revealed that this is the biggest change I’ve made to my approach. Not just for AI search, but for traditional SEO.

    Recent findings suggest that I don’t begin by asking which prompts a brand should appear in. Or how much search volume a keyword or even topic has. Mainly because my trust in search volume and all forms of visibility is at rock bottom.

    So I use SparkToro to investigate where audiences spend time, which websites they visit, who influences them, and which platforms they’re disproportionately likely to use compared with the wider population.

    For this audience, I know that if I want to influence them, LinkedIn is a non-negotiable (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Industry observers note that I combine that with traditional search research, AI search behaviour and an assessment of the brand’s existing positioning. You don’t need to overcomplicate this – ask a number of different LLMs about insert brand and record the responses.

    I want to answer some relatively straightforward questions:.

    This research should inform two things.

    First, our owned platforms. We use what we’ve learned to improve the way we position ourselves, the services we offer, the language we use, and the content we create.

    Let’s try to make things under our control as human and well-targeted as possible.

    In a recent development, second, our wider marketing strategy. We identify the publications, communities, creators, platforms, and people capable of influencing that audience, and decide how to reach them.

    Audience affinity with specific Subreddits, via SparkToro (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Sources indicate that you need to know this. Not because it might get your brand mentioned as part of the training data. But because this is where you should be marketing.

    Sources indicate that made-up prompt data is out. Real, human-led marketing is in. If we want SEO to be taken seriously, this is the proper evolution.

    Recent findings suggest that the goal isn’t to manufacture mentions for an AI model. It’s to build a brand people want to discover, engage with, and recommend.

    According to recent reports, if those activities also increase your representation in AI systems, wonderful. But that’s a delicious byproduct, not the reason for doing them.

    While audience research informs the wider strategy, your website needs to be accessible, understandable, and representative of who you are. That is something reasonably competent SEOs can lead.

    Can the relevant search and AI crawlers access your content? Can they render it? Are you inadvertently blocking systems you want to reach?

    This means reviewing bot management, robots directives, rendering, indexability, internal linking, site architecture, and the usual technical SEO fundamentals.

    A traditional SEO-type audit with a few improvements.

    Industry observers note that one that understands that not all AI bots serve the same purpose. Training crawlers, search crawlers, and user-triggered retrieval systems can have different access requirements and commercial implications.

    Crawlers do different things (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    Especially crucial if you’re working for – or with – a publisher. Someone whose business may depend on you understanding the wider context.

    If you’re restricting access to your content, you need to understand what you’re giving up, what you’re protecting, and where the value might exist instead.

    Perhaps that’s content licensing, direct audience relationships or proprietary products.

    The role of the SEO changes considerably in an environment where you’re not maximising access. You’re helping the business understand the trade-offs between visibility, intellectual property and commercial value.

    It’s like a paywall. You’re restricting reach for commercial purposes. It’s the correct move if played properly.

    See Cyrus Shepherd’s excellent test to understand how much search traffic was truly influenced by Google’s AI proposition.

    According to recent reports, this is where I think modern information retrieval methods and SEO intersect perfectly. I’ve written about how to approach this in Entities Are the Foundation of Modern SEO.

    This framework is relatively simple:.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    This isn’t about adding some structured data and hoping ChatGPT tries to hump your leg. Spoiler: It won’t.

    It’s about making sure that your owned presence accurately represents your positioning and that the wider internet provides credible, independent evidence to support it.

    Industry observers note that so, we know who we are. We’ve represented ourselves properly. Now we have to rely on *shudders* other people to corroborate this message.

    We have to build an off-site presence.

    This references a podcast I did with Andy Francos and an article I wrote for Lumar two years ago (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    According to recent reports, we’re talking actual, real marketing (not SEO). PR, partnerships, content and audience development.

    If the people you’re trying to reach spend their time reading particular publications, following particular experts or participating in particular communities, those are the places worth investing in.

    Bollocks to a citation. Your audience is there. You know, people you could actually sell something to.

    That might mean publishing original research, collaborating with influential people, appearing on podcasts, creating genuinely useful resources or contributing expertise to relevant publications.

    In a recent development, some of those activities will generate links. Others will generate mentions, relationships, conversations and brand demand – a real representation of site quality in Google.

    The more consistently you’re associated with the right subjects, people and organizations, the stronger your wider digital presence can become. That is, in essence, how training data and entity relationships work.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    If you’re lucky, some of that evidence may eventually influence how AI systems represent you.

    But you won’t care, because you’ll have been making sales by marketing to actual customers.

    Modern methods of information retrieval across SEO and AI search share many, if not all of the same fundamentals.

    It has been revealed that arguably, AI search has a longer tail to it. But it’s not sustainable, nor sensible, to create a page for every possible thought your audience may have. To perpetuate a false Henry Ford quote:.

    “If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses.” H. Ford, Never.

    Industry observers note that so you need to strike a balance. No one cares about visibility without impact. At least not for long.

    In a recent development, there is room to try and test things. Good things. Things real people will care about.

    Recent findings suggest that people like Jan-Willem Bobbink and Dan Petrovic highlight some really brilliant things you can test that are eminently sensible for SEO and AI search. Surprise, surprise, they work for people too. It’s marketing.

    Industry observers note that let me give you an example. Maybe more accurately, let me steal one of Jan’s:.

    It has been revealed that “I spent the last three weeks on SEO / GEO work for B2B clients, and the changes that made the biggest difference were mostly about information that was missing or hard to find. Buyers run into the same problems on these sites, so you can usually get these fixes approved without having to explain SEO to anyone.”.

    Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

    Being explicit, consistent, and accurate is not an AI hack. It’s just pretty sensible.

    Sources indicate that adding pricing pages, case studies, and telling people why you are the best in the business are always good ideas. Even if your pricing pages just say something like prices starting at x, that is a better way of finding the right audience.

    And if you want to feature in AI responses, for god’s sake don’t hide your case studies. You need to provide a clear reason for your inclusion. Hard if your best work is hidden.

    Statements like “Client Y saw a 30% improvement in deliverability metrics” can noticeably improve your citation rate because a model is literally looking for a reason to include you. You need to give them one. Just as you would a person.

    Recent findings suggest that experience. Expertise. Authority. Trust. Not so stupid after all.

    Measurement’s been broken for a decade anyway. It’s just nice for the C-suite to have numbers to report on – even if they’re complete hokum.

    You try and figure this out (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    It has been revealed that AI visibility’s not much better. A hugely flawed metric given the personalization, lack of prompt data, and completely individual prompts. But it’s better than nothing. Indicative at best, but you need to use something.

    Recent findings suggest that people still want to know how they’re represented in AI systems. And so they should – it’s a valuable channel. My preference is to establish a representative set of prompts across four areas:.

    Track these consistently across the systems that matter to your audience.

    Industry observers note that look at whether you’re mentioned, how you’re described, which competitors appear, and which sources are being used. Find out when you start to appear for certain terms and see if it matches your positioning.

    I always track my mentions with Alertmouse (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    I appear in AI recommendations around news SEO expertise despite having done nothing specifically to optimize for AI search.

    What I have done is spend years working in the industry, publishing, building relationships, contributing expertise, and establishing a reasonably clear on-site and off-site identity.

    Not a bad list, although I am not sure ChatGPT is quite nailing the profile pictures for us… (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

    I guarantee you, if you ask Barry Adams, he’ll tell you he’s done nothing special for AI either.

    I’ve written what I think are high-quality articles on third-party websites and podcasts, featured in roundups, and built my own distribution platform. It just also happens to work for featuring in AI systems.

    AI systems don’t necessarily need to send you traffic to influence commercial outcomes. Which is a good thing, because ChatGPT sends less than 1% of Google’s traffic.

    Similarweb’s research found that users who received a brand recommendation in ChatGPT were 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand’s website within the following seven days than users who were recommended a competitor.

    Sources indicate that much of that activity happened through subsequent branded searches rather than direct AI referrals. One of those measures of site quality that should be monitored.

    AI search can and does function as a brand discovery and consideration channel. I think referral traffic is, at best, a secondary measure of success from LLMs. While they’ve engineered the exit out, you cannot deny the reach these systems have.

    Unfortunately, our attribution systems can’t cope with “I saw it here once.” We need to focus on incremental change. The outcomes attributable to marketing.

    Establish a baseline. Run a campaign. Measure changes in branded demand, direct visits, conversions, leads, and commercial outcomes. Compare with appropriate benchmarks or control groups where possible.

    Keep tracking AI visibility, referrals and citations, but use them as supporting indicators.

    Our objective is to establish whether mentioned marketing activity is creating additional business value, not whether ChatGPT has linked to your homepage.

    For businesses whose models depend on monetizing information and attracting a click, AI search presents a very different challenge.

    It has been revealed that they are monetizing other people’s work for their own ill-gotten gain. That is an irrefutable commercial dilemma. Hence all the protectionism. So we need to establish what that cost is and try to find alternative methods of monetization.

    In The Generative AI Report Sucks – Let’s Make It Brilliant, I outlined how publishers can combine AI visibility data with traffic dependency, commercial value, audience resilience, and server logs.

    We can go some way toward solving actual business problems.

    In a recent development, always, always, always a good thing to do. Regardless of your job.

    It has been revealed that this opportunity is no different, especially for organizations (like publishers) with substantial authority across particular subjects. They have influence within the wider information ecosystem.

    That influence can have commercial value.

    Industry observers note that publishers Should Think About AI Visibility. Content licensing, data partnerships, research collaborations, and other commercial arrangements offer opportunities to monetize expertise and proprietary information.

    But this needs careful handling.

    According to recent reports, selling links or undisclosed editorial influence is not a sustainable AI strategy. It introduces reputational, editorial, and search-policy risks.

    The more sustainable opportunity is to understand the value of your existing content, expertise, audience, and distribution – and build legitimate commercial products around those assets.

    Lots of companies are selling or actively considering selling their archived assets or data to AI companies:.

    For publishers in particular, this is an opportunity to rethink the value they create beyond the click. See the Daily Mail’s approach to GEO monetization here.

    If you’re more on the glass half full side, you’ll be able to sniff out commercial opportunities. Ideally ones that don’t ruin the brand or fall foul of Google’s link payment guidelines.

    General advice: If something smells a bit off, it probably is.

    If you’re a business looking to take this seriously, there’s an organizational question you need to answer.

    Who is responsible for all of this?

    Because as great as we can be, it shouldn’t just be your SEO.

    This touches technical infrastructure, audience research, brand positioning, content, PR, distribution, commercial partnerships, and measurement. That requires someone who understands the entire ecosystem and, crucially, how to influence people.

    Industry observers note that nobody is an expert at all of these things. They’re too different. Too complex.

    For larger businesses, I’d be thinking about a Head of Marketing or Head of Discoverability with responsibility for coordinating these activities. Someone who at least knows the basics of each and can herd a clowder of cats.

    They need the authority to bring different teams together, allocate resources, challenge existing assumptions and measure outcomes against business objectives.

    Sources indicate that there’s a reason SEOs rarely graduate to marketing lead positions. We don’t understand wider marketing because we’ve rarely had to. SEO was always the best channel… According to wonky data, anyway.

    AI search gives us a very good reason to change that.

    And for anyone working in SEO, I think there are three particularly interesting directions.

    All three have tremendous value. Limiting yourself to SEO, particularly as a collection of search-engine or LLM-specific tactics, is increasingly short-sighted.

    According to recent reports, discoverability has been changing for a decade. We need to think much more broadly about how audiences discover and engage with content. The opportunity is to bring those disciplines together.

    A little rebrand and refocus on what you want from your career may be the best thing you ever do.

    Sources indicate that stop trying to engineer your way into an AI response. Build a brand worth recommending, an audience worth owning, and a business that benefits whether the citation comes or not.

    Enjoy yourself. This will be a better era for marketers and marketing. Your competition is lazy and inept. They’re just faster.

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    In a recent development, the newly introduced budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    According to recent reports, A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    Industry observers note that that changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    Recent findings suggest that “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan said. “They see what Substantial Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s massive local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a upcoming tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    It has been revealed that the labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan remarked.

    There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    Industry observers note that in the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    But News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    The Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Launched in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results demonstrated the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    Industry observers note that “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said.

    According to recent reports, some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    Deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan mentioned.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    It has been revealed that “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    According to recent reports, at the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    Sources indicate that LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson noted.

    OpenNews remarked in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    The future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    In a recent development, the three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he stated. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    Microsoft Rebuilds Its Smart Bidding Prediction Models, Rolling Out Automatically via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Microsoft Advertising is rolling out what it calls its biggest bidding model upgrade in a decade.
    • Microsoft will apply the upgrade automatically as it reaches more accounts.
    • Recent findings suggest that microsoft says the new models can change how quickly campaigns spend and how closely they stick to your targets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft Advertising is rolling out what it calls its biggest bidding model upgrade in a decade. The new models use more signals to predict whether an ad click will turn into a conversion and what it might be worth.

    Microsoft will apply the upgrade automatically as it reaches more accounts. That means campaigns can start spending differently before you make any changes yourself. Microsoft announced the rollout on November 18 and prepares more bidding updates in 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that microsoft says the new models can change how quickly campaigns spend and how closely they stick to your targets. These are the areas to keep an eye on:.

    Industry observers note that A $50 CPA target still leaves room for a campaign to bring in conversions at $40 each, even if it spends its full budget. A max CPC can limit that flexibility. Say you average $3 a click and cap bids at $5. The cap rules out a $6 bid even if Microsoft expects the click could bring in a conversion within your CPA target.

    Say you raise your CPA target on Monday and customers usually take a week to buy. By Friday, you know what Monday’s clicks cost, but you may still be waiting on some of the sales. Faster bidding won’t shorten the time those customers take to buy.

    Industry observers note that raising a CPA target or lowering a ROAS target can open up auctions your campaign previously passed up. To limit swings in performance, Microsoft suggests making those changes in 15% increments and reviewing each after one conversion cycle. For a bigger change, like switching bid strategies or adding a conversion goal, Microsoft recommends allowing one to two cycles.

    Microsoft recommends conversion-based bidding for fresh campaigns once the account has at least five conversions. Those can come from campaigns you already run. If you’re still gathering your first five, Enhanced CPC is an option.

    It has been revealed that on LinkedIn, Sophie Westall asked if the same advice applies to low-volume accounts already using Enhanced CPC. Microsoft Advertising Liaison Navah Hopkins replied:.

    Every account is different so a blanket recommendation still needs to be put to the test. With that said, so long as the account has at least 5 conversions total, the system is smart enough to use that to begin with conversion-based bidding. While we still recommend the 30-day evaluation period and not making too many changes if you’re working with fewer conversions, the system is much more responsive now!

    For judging performance, Microsoft recommends around 30 conversions in 30 days at the campaign or portfolio level. A low-volume campaign can reach the end of that first month and still have too few conversions to judge the switch.

    Microsoft reported 10% more conversion value per click at roughly the same ROAS after the model upgrade. That result came from August 2026 global Search and Audience Network data for advertisers using Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS.

    Sources indicate that microsoft also looked at advertisers who switched bid strategies. Search advertisers who moved from Target CPA to Target ROAS saw 8% more conversion value at a similar ROAS. Advertisers who moved from Enhanced CPC to Maximize Conversions with a CPA target saw 18% more conversions at a similar CPA.

    If you’re considering Target ROAS, pull up a few recent purchases in Microsoft Advertising and compare the reported values with the order totals. A $40 order and a $400 order can both show up as conversions even if your tracking assigns them the same value. That’s easy to miss if you’re used to checking that purchases are coming through and leaving it there.

    Recent findings suggest that microsoft reported its largest gains from value-based bidding among advertisers who sent actual transaction values. If your purchase goal uses a fixed value, the reported ROAS reflects that estimate. It can move as you sell more or spend less, but it won’t capture a change in how much customers spend per order.

    With lead gen, you may need time to get a better read on what a conversion is worth. Two people can submit the same form, and sales may find out a week later that only one is a fit.

    Pedro Bailaderia asked Navah Hopkins about sending an estimate at submission and updating it once more information comes into the CRM. Hopkins supported using the Conversions API or offline imports. She also advised setting a ROAS target that reflects the values you send.

    If your team is still working out how to value a qualified lead, that’s worth settling before you set a ROAS target. A campaign can hit the target you set while sales is still waiting for more leads it can work with.

    In a recent development, if a campaign already brings in the sales or leads you need at a cost you’re happy with, you can give the upgrade some room before changing anything. Keeping your settings steady makes it easier to see how the new models work with the goals and budget you already have.

    The rollout may be more useful if you’ve been adjusting targets to get a campaign to spend more evenly. If delivery settles down on its own, you may have fewer reasons to touch those targets during the week. That would leave you freer to change them when the business needs more volume or can afford to pay more for a conversion.

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.     According to recent reports, most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause rapidly and explain it in plain language. We're looking for a Deliverability and Compliance Specialist to own deliverability support for that long tail of creators, run Kit's abuse desk, and make the compliance calls that protect the sending reputation every creator on Kit shares.

    It has been revealed that you'll also build the playbooks, training, and AI-assisted workflows that help Support and contractors handle more deliverability questions on their own, and you'll partner with our infrastructure engineers as we run more of our sending in-house. A creator can't build a lasting business if their emails don't arrive, so this work connects directly to our mission.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes digging through headers and bounce logs to find the real cause of a problem, can explain DMARC alignment to a first-time creator without jargon, and is comfortable making a firm call when a situation is gray. You don't wait for someone to tell you what needs fixing. You proactively spot opportunities, identify patterns, and take the initiative to improve deliverability before problems arise.

    You'll report to Alyssa Dulin, Director of Creator Success, and collaborate closely with:.

    Our Deliverability team: a Deliverability Lead who supports our highest-value accounts and leads deliverability education, and a Deliverability Specialist who onboards and ramps up large senders moving to Kit.

    Our infrastructure engineers, who run Kit's sending infrastructure.

    Our compliance and anti-abuse engineers, who build the automated checks that keep spammers off Kit.

    Product Specialists and the Support team, who handle the front line and escalate deliverability challenges to you.

    Customer Success Managers (we call them Creator Growth Managers at Kit), Sales and Migrations, and Product Managers.

    In a recent development, first Week: Get set up in Kit, our admin tools, and our support and ticketing systems, and meet our distributed team in Get To Know You chats (GTKYs). Meet the deliverability team and get an introduction on the current projects. Read our deliverability playbooks and SOPs, and get access to the monitoring tools you'll use every day: Google Postmaster Tools, Microsoft SNDS, blocklist monitoring, and our internal delivery dashboards.

    Recent findings suggest that first Month: Shadow the Deliverability team and Product Specialists on deliverability tickets, account approvals, and abuse reports, then start answering queue tickets with review. Join the daily monitoring rotation (blocklist delisting, Postmaster and delivery monitoring) and the weekly Deliverability team meeting. Learn how account approvals, compliance flags, and our in-house sending platform work. By the end of the month, work deliverability tickets and abuse reports on your own and send your first delisting requests. Project: build a recurring report showing the trending deliverability ticket reasons so we understand what’s causing how to reduce friction for customers and how to solve it.

    Sources indicate that first Six Months: Own the deliverability support queue for creators without a dedicated CGM: spam-folder placement, bounces, authentication and DMARC setup, and escalations from Product Specialists. Own compliance end to end, from upcoming-account approvals and compliance flags to pausing or closing accounts that put our shared reputation at risk.Run Kit's abuse desk. You'll write and share a strategy that covers coverage, response-time targets, escalation paths, and quality checks, then put it in place so routine spam, phishing, and blocklist reports follow clear SOPs while you take the hardest cases yourself. Be the go-to contact for day-to-day mailbox provider complications with Microsoft, Gmail, Yahoo, Comcast, and regional providers, and write an incident runbook for blocklistings and provider throttling. Track the queue with a simple scorecard (volume, first response time, and escalation rate) and share what you learn with the team. Run training sessions for Support and ship your first process or AI improvements, like cleaner ticket categorization or better account data for our AI support agent, so more deliverability tickets get solved without escalation..

    Industry observers note that first Year: Deliverability support is faster and more consistent for every creator on Kit, including the ones who never talk to a CGM.     Deep working knowledge of email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, alignment, and BIMI basics), plus the ability to read raw message headers and SMTP bounce and deferral codes.

    Hands-on use of Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS/JMRP, and comfort working with major blocklists (Spamhaus, Abusix, Barracuda, Spamcop, and others) and their delisting processes.

    • This guide will help you understand how robots.txt rules work so you can avoid common robots.txt mistakes, keep useful content accessible, but at the same time limit unnecessary crawling.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The robots.txt file has always been an essential tool for managing crawler access to a website. With AI search tools and agents now visiting websites alongside traditional crawlers, you need to know which rules each one follows.

    Industry observers note that but, blocking the wrong bot can exclude your content from LLMs or SERPs, while leaving unnecessary URLs open can waste crawl budget on large sites. So, you need to know what you are doing.

    This guide will help you understand how robots.txt rules work so you can avoid common robots.txt mistakes, keep useful content accessible, but at the same time limit unnecessary crawling.

    The robots.txt is a simple text file that sits in the root directory of your site and tells crawlers what should be crawled.

    The table below provides a quick reference to the key robots.txt directives.

    This 2024 screenshot shows an example of robots.txt from ikea.com with multiple rules.

    Note that robots.txt doesn’t support full regular expressions and only has two wildcards:.

    Also, note that URL path matching is case-sensitive, e.g., “filter=” is not equal to “Filter=.” The directive names and user-agent matching are case-insensitive.

    When setting up a robots.txt file, it’s crucial to know the order in which search engines decide which rules to apply in case of conflicting rules.

    When you write a separate set of rules for a bot, it follows those rules instead of the rules under User-agent: *. For example:.

    It has been revealed that here, Googlebot can crawl /private/ because its own rules allow every URL to be crawled. To block that directory for Googlebot, add Disallow: /private/ beneath its Allow: / line.

    Within the applicable group, Google follows these two key rules:.

    Recent findings suggest that the rule that matches more characters in the URL will be applied. For example:.

    In this case, the “Allow: /downloads/free/” rule is more specific than “Disallow: /downloads/” because it targets a subdirectory.

    Google will allow crawling of subfolder “/downloads/free/” but block everything else under “/downloads/.”.

    When multiple rules are equally specific, for example:.

    Google will choose the least restrictive one. This means Google will allow access to /downloads/.

    Google’s 2024 reminder about action URLs focused on add-to-cart and wishlist links that waste crawler and server resources.

    Imagine you have an online store with hundreds of thousands of pages. There are sections of websites like filtered pages that may have an infinite number of versions. Those pages don’t have unique value, essentially contain duplicate content, and may create infinite crawl space, thus wasting your server and Googlebot’s resources. That is where robots.txt comes in, preventing search engine bots from crawling those pages.

    If you don’t do that, Google may try to crawl an infinite number of URLs with different (even non-existent) search parameter values, causing spikes and a waste of crawl budget.

    As a general rule, you should always ask why certain pages exist, and whether they have any value for search engines to crawl and index.

    Depending on your site and indexing goals, candidates for crawl restrictions include:.

    Let’s dive into examples of how you can use robots.txt for each case.

    According to recent reports, internal search results are a common source of unnecessary crawling by Google and other search engines. If those results are not intended to appear in search, consider restricting their crawl space.

    On WordPress websites, it is usually an “s” parameter, and the URL looks like this:.

    Gary Illyes from Google has repeatedly warned to block “action” URLs as they can cause Googlebot to crawl them indefinitely even non-existent URLs with different combinations.

    Here is the rule you can use in your robots.txt to block such URLs from being crawled:.

    This crawl-stats screenshot, included in the original 2024 guide, illustrates reduced crawling of non-existent internal search URLs after they were blocked via robots.txt.

    Note that Google may index blocked pages based on links to their URLs. Robots.txt does not guarantee their removal from search. If removal is your goal, use noindex and allow Google to crawl the page so it can read that instruction.

    Recent findings suggest that faceted navigation is an integral part of every ecommerce website. There can be cases where faceted navigation is part of an SEO strategy and aimed at ranking for general product searches.

    Recent findings suggest that zalando’s color-based landing pages, such as those targeting “gray t-shirt” illustrate this approach. The principle is to keep useful search landing pages crawlable while restricting unwanted filter combinations.

    However, in most cases, this is not the case, and filter parameters are used merely for filtering products, creating dozens of pages with duplicate content.

    There may be multiple filter parameters in one URL. Identify which ones generate unwanted crawl space; do not block facets that form part of your search strategy. Google’s faceted-navigation guidance distinguishes these two cases.

    For example, if you have filters with the following parameters “sortby,” “color,” and “price,” you may use this set of rules:.

    These pairs match each parameter in the first position or after another parameter. Add only the parameters you intend to restrict, and test both wanted and unwanted URLs.

    UTM parameters are used for tracking purposes.

    In the Reddit exchange shown below, John Mueller addressed tracking parameters on external links. Keep that context separate from internally generated filter or search URLs.

    It has been revealed that keep internal links pointed at the URLs you want crawled. Decide whether to block a parameter by what it does on your site; the presence of a query string alone is not a reason to disallow a page.

    Let’s say you have a lot of PDF documents, such as product guides, brochures, or downloadable papers, and you don’t want them crawled.

    Here is a simple robots.txt rule that will block search engine bots from accessing those documents:.

    The “Disallow: /*.pdf$” line tells crawlers not to crawl any URLs that end with .pdf.

    In a recent development, by using /*, the rule matches any path on the website. As a result, any URL ending with .pdf will be blocked from crawling. It will not match /guide.pdf?download=1 or an uppercase .PDF extension; test any such variants separately. If you want a PDF excluded from search, use an X-Robots-Tag: noindex HTTP header and keep it crawlable so Google can read the header.

    If you have a WordPress website and want to disallow PDFs from the uploads directory where you upload them via the CMS, you can use the following rule:.

    You can see that we have conflicting rules here.

    In case of conflicting rules, the more specific one takes priority, which means the last line ensures that only the specific file located in folder “wp-content/uploads/2024/09/allowed-document.pdf” is allowed to be crawled.

    Let’s say you have an API endpoint where you submit your data from the form. It is likely your form has an action attribute like action=”/form/submissions/.”.

    According to recent reports, if a crawler discovers the URL /form/submissions/, you may want to prevent crawling of that path. You can request that with this rule:.

    By specifying a directory in the Disallow rule, you are telling the crawlers to avoid crawling all pages under that directory, and you don’t need to use the (*) wildcard anymore, like “/form/*.”.

    Note that you must always specify relative paths and never absolute URLs, like “https://www.example.com/form/” for Disallow and Allow directives.

    Be cautious to avoid malformed rules. For example, using /form without a trailing slash will also match a page /form-design-examples/, which may be a page on your blog that you want to index.

    Read: 8 Common Robots.txt Issues And How To Fix Them.

    If you have an ecommerce website, you likely have directories that start with “/myaccount/,” such as “/myaccount/orders/” or “/myaccount/profile/.”.

    With the top page “/myaccount/” being a sign-in page that you want to be indexed and found by consumers in search, you may want to disallow the subpages from being crawled by Googlebot.

    You can use the Disallow rule in combination with the Allow rule to block everything under the “/myaccount/” directory (except the /myaccount/ page).

    And again, since Google uses the most specific rule, it will disallow everything under the /myaccount/ directory but allow only the /myaccount/ page to be crawled.

    Here’s another use case of combining the Disallow and Allow rules: in case you have your search under the /search/ directory and want it to be found and indexed but block actual search URLs:.

    Every website uses JavaScript, and many of these scripts are not related to the rendering of content, such as tracking scripts or those used for loading AdSense.

    Industry observers note that only block a script after confirming it is unnecessary for rendering the content and links you want indexed. Use URL Inspection to check the rendered page; blocking a shared bundle or a script with rendering dependencies can prevent Google from seeing vital content. A robots.txt file on your host also cannot control a script fetched from a different host.

    Below is a sample line that is disallowing sample JavaScript, which contains tracking pixels.

    According to recent reports, you can block training bots while allowing AI tools to find your pages and retrieve them for users. The key is to give training, search, and user-requested AI crawlers separate rules.

    It has been revealed that publishers may block training to limit the use of their reporting without attribution, while ecommerce brands may welcome it if product mentions lead people to search and buy. Because the benefits differ by business, developers should set these rules with stakeholders.

    Sources indicate that disallowing training bots cannot guarantee that your content stays out of training datasets, because crawlers that ignore robots.txt can still collect it. It also does not force AI tools to visit or cite your site, as they may find the information elsewhere.

    Sources indicate that A BuzzStream study covered by SEJ in January 2026, found that 79% of the US and UK news sites examined disallowed at least one training bot, while 71% disallowed at least one retrieval or live-search bot. Because retrieval helps AI tools find and cite your pages, blocking those bots is a separate decision from opting out of training.

    Sources indicate that openAI uses OAI-SearchBot to surface websites in ChatGPT search answers, while ChatGPT-User handles user-requested visits. Because search and training permissions are separate, you can allow OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User while blocking GPTBot.

    This example blocks OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s training crawlers while allowing their search and user-requested bots, along with Perplexity’s:.

    Sources indicate that in the example above, /private/ is an excluded directory. Replace it with any paths you want to keep those bots from crawling.

    Most major AI crawlers follow robots.txt, including OpenAI’s GPTBot and Anthropic’s ClaudeBot.

    User-requested visits work differently because some providers allow their bots to bypass robots.txt or generally ignore it when acting on a user’s request. OpenAI says robots.txt may not apply to ChatGPT-User, and Perplexity says Perplexity-User generally ignores it. Anthropic says its bots, including Claude-User, honor robots.txt. Because robots.txt only tells bots which URLs they may crawl, you need authentication to protect private content.

    The bot tokens and robots.txt policies for Copilot’s browser visits, Grok, DeepSeek, and Meta Muse remain unknown because I could not verify them in the providers’ public documentation.

    Google and Apple provide separate robots.txt tokens for controlling how crawled content is used:.

    In a recent development, google-Extended covers Gemini training and specified grounding uses, where source content helps generate an answer. Blocking it does not block Googlebot or affect ordinary Google Search inclusion. Applebot-Extended controls foundation-model training without blocking Applebot’s search crawl. Neither token is a separate crawler, so these rules do not reduce crawling requests by themselves.

    After changing the file, check your server log files and confirm that your firewall allows the bots you want. Use server or CDN controls when you need to enforce access restrictions.

    For background, see SEJ’s earlier coverage of AI content use and AI chatbot traffic.

    Including your sitemap URL in the robots.txt file helps search engines easily discover all the notable pages on your website. This is done by adding a specific line that points to your sitemap location, and you can specify multiple sitemaps, each on its own line.

    Unlike Allow or Disallow rules, which allow only a relative path, the Sitemap directive requires a full, absolute URL to indicate the location of the sitemap.

    Ensure the sitemaps’ URLs are accessible to search engines and have proper syntax to avoid errors.

    The crawl-delay directive in robots.txt specifies the number of seconds a bot should wait before crawling the next page. While Googlebot does not recognize the crawl-delay directive, other bots may respect it.

    It helps prevent server overload by controlling how frequently bots crawl your site.

    For example, if you want ClaudeBot to crawl your content for AI training but want to avoid server overload, you can set a crawl delay to manage the interval between requests.

    Industry observers note that this requests a 60-second delay from ClaudeBot, which Anthropic documents as supporting the non-standard Crawl-delay extension. Use this when you intend to allow that crawl. Adding a delay does not override a Disallow: / rule for the same bot; review the complete group rather than copying both policies.

    In a recent development, of course, there may be AI bots that don’t respect crawl delay directives. In that case, you may need to use a web firewall to rate limit them.

    Once you’ve composed your robots.txt, you can use these tools to troubleshoot if the syntax is correct or if you didn’t accidentally block an important URL.

    Once you’ve updated your robots.txt, you must check whether it contains any error or accidentally blocks URLs you want to be crawled, such as resources, images, or website sections.

    In a recent development, navigate to Settings > robots.txt to open the robots.txt report. It highlights the files Google fetched and any parsing warnings or errors. You can request a recrawl after a critical change. To test whether an individual page is blocked, use URL Inspection.

    The video below illustrates the report workflow; interface details may differ from the current version.

    Google’s robots.txt parser is an open-source parser and matcher based on the implementation used in Google’s crawler.

    According to recent reports, it requires advanced skills to install and run on your local computer. But it is highly recommended to take time and do it as instructed on that page because you can validate your changes in the robots.txt file before uploading to your server in line with the official Google parser.

    Robots.txt rules apply to the host, protocol, and port where the file is requested. If you need crawl restrictions on a subdomain, its robots.txt URL must serve the rules or redirect to a file that does; the parent domain’s file is not inherited.

    It creates challenges when you have a website with a dozen subdomains, as it means you should maintain a bunch of robots.txt files separately.

    However, it is possible to host a robots.txt file on a subdomain, such as https://cdn.example.com/robots.txt, and set up a redirect from https://www.example.com/robots.txt to it.

    You can do vice versa and host it only under the root domain and redirect from subdomains to the root.

    Google applies the retrieved rules to the host that originally requested robots.txt, not automatically to the host storing the shared file. Configure a redirect from each host you want to manage, and check that the shared paths make sense for all of them.

    According to recent reports, it helps make updates and maintenance more efficient. Otherwise, you would need to use a separate robots.txt file for each subdomain.

    A properly optimized robots.txt file is crucial for managing a website’s crawl budget. It ensures that search engines like Googlebot spend their time on valuable pages rather than wasting resources on unnecessary ones.

    According to recent reports, blocking compliant crawlers can reduce unwanted requests. For AI systems, distinguish crawl restrictions from training-use controls, and verify the effect in your logs. Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended do not stop a separate crawler.

    Make sure you always validate your changes to avoid unexpected crawlability problems.

    However, remember that crawl demand and serving capacity both matter. Useful content, efficient page loading, and a healthy server remain notable alongside robots.txt rules.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The Cornell Daily Sun saw traffic spike by almost 500% in September.

    RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop. For July, August, and September, traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data.

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEHow did newspapers in places like Harrisburg, Birmingham, and Syracuse become some of America’s most-read online?Joshua BentonJuly 23, 2025A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com. Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com, Mlive.com, and NJ.com, among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025.

    According to recent reports, still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a fresh website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia. The parent company is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney mentioned.

    Sources indicate that in Florida, Cape Coral Breeze, a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “Best of Cape Coral” contest, where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website consumers to our news coverage,” Eckenrode said, and had some success with that strategy.

    Industry observers note that in September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in Newly introduced York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump.

    On the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. “Our traffic is volatile like everyone else’s, but we had a strong September mainly because a couple of stories performed very well,” noted Annika Toernqvist, MediaNews Group’s managing editor for digital for Northern California. Environmental beat reporter Paul Rogers‘ story about a upcoming California law that will ban watering artificial turf “performed exceptionally well on Google and Google Discovery”; 62% of traffic to the story came from search. Stories about the local impact of new state laws consistently do well with the outlet’s readers, according to Toernqvist, and this was “a hot topic with a strong headline.” The story was also the top subscription converter in September. Another story by Rogers covering the proposed renaming of Fremont State Park also drove traffic that month; 86% came from search, mostly from Google Discovery.

    It has been revealed that meanwhile, celebrity reporter Martha Ross‘ story about a latest book on King Charles’ valet performed well in part thanks to a bump from…the Drudge Report. (“Yes, the Drudge Report still drives traffic,” Toernqvist said; it accounted for 43% of visits to that story.).
